[id="agent-state-persistence-langgraph_{context}"]
= Agent state persistence for LangGraph agents

[role="_abstract"]
You can configure persistent state backends for LangGraph agents on {productname-long} to ensure that conversation history, agent checkpoints, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) context survive pod restarts and scaling events.
Without persistent state, agents lose all in-progress conversations and accumulated context when a pod is rescheduled, which causes failures in production workloads that require continuity.

LangGraph agents maintain state at two layers: short-term checkpoints that track individual conversation threads, and long-term memory that persists context across threads.
Understanding these layers helps you choose the right storage backend for your workload and configure the Llama Stack provider swap from local to production storage.

== Two-layer state model

LangGraph agents separate state into two layers, each serving a different purpose.

Short-term checkpoints (thread-level)::
Checkpoints capture the state of a LangGraph graph execution at each node change within a single conversation thread.
Each checkpoint records the graph node, input, output, and any accumulated state variables for a specific `thread_id`.
+
In local development, checkpoints use the `MemorySaver` class, which stores state in the Python process memory.
When the process stops, all checkpoint data is lost.
+
In production, checkpoints move to durable storage backends such as PostgreSQL or Redis, which persist data independently of the agent pod lifecycle.

Long-term memory (cross-thread)::
Long-term memory enables agents to retain information across multiple conversation threads.
This includes user preferences, accumulated knowledge, and RAG document context that should persist beyond a single conversation session.
+
The Llama Stack memory API abstracts long-term memory storage behind a provider interface.
In local development, the `inline::meta-reference` provider stores memory in SQLite.
In production, the same API routes memory operations to PostgreSQL through configuration changes in the `run.yaml` file.

== Local storage backends

In local development, LangGraph agents use lightweight, ephemeral storage backends that require no external services.

`MemorySaver`:: The default LangGraph checkpointer for local development.
Stores all state in the Python process memory.
Data is lost when the process exits.
Suitable only for development and testing.

SQLite:: The Llama Stack `inline::meta-reference` provider stores agent metadata, response history, and memory in SQLite databases on the local filesystem.
The `run.yaml` configuration specifies the file paths through the `persistence_store` and `responses_store` settings.
SQLite databases persist across process restarts but are not suitable for multi-instance or multi-pod deployments.

== Production storage backends

Production deployments require storage backends that persist data independently of the agent pod lifecycle and support concurrent access from multiple pods.

PostgreSQL::
The recommended production backend for both Llama Stack metadata and LangGraph checkpoints.
PostgreSQL provides ACID transactions, concurrent access support, and integration with {productname-short} backup and monitoring tools.
+
You can configure PostgreSQL as the storage backend in two ways:
+
* Set `persistence_store.type: postgres` in the `run.yaml` `providers.agents` section to store Llama Stack agent metadata in PostgreSQL.
* Use the LangGraph `PostgresSaver` checkpointer in your agent application code to store graph checkpoints in PostgreSQL.
+
Both approaches can point to the same PostgreSQL instance or use separate instances depending on isolation requirements.

Redis::
An alternative production backend for LangGraph checkpoints.
Redis provides low-latency key-value storage suitable for high-throughput agent workloads.
+
Use the LangGraph `RedisSaver` checkpointer in your agent application code.
Redis does not replace the Llama Stack metadata store, which still requires PostgreSQL or SQLite.

== How the Llama Stack memory API abstracts the storage swap

The Llama Stack memory API provides a consistent interface for memory operations regardless of the underlying storage backend.
Your agent application code calls the same API methods (for example, `memory_banks.create()`, `memory.insert()`, `memory.query()`) in both local and production environments.

The storage backend is determined by the `providers.agents` section in the `run.yaml` configuration file.
Changing the `persistence_store.type` from `sqlite` to `postgres` and providing connection parameters is the only modification required.
The agent application code does not change.

For LangGraph-native checkpointers (`MemorySaver`, `PostgresSaver`, `RedisSaver`), the swap is performed in the agent application code by changing the checkpointer class instantiation.
This is typically a single-line change in the application entry point.

== Llama Stack memory API and LangGraph checkpointer comparison

LangGraph agents on {productname-short} can use two approaches for state persistence, and the approaches are complementary.

Llama Stack memory API path::
Use this approach for Llama Stack agent metadata, response history, and cross-thread memory.
The storage backend is configured in `run.yaml` and does not require code changes.

LangGraph checkpointer path::
Use this approach for graph execution checkpoints within a single conversation thread.
The checkpointer class is set in the agent application code.
Use `PostgresSaver` or `RedisSaver` for production deployments.

In many production deployments, you use both approaches together.
The Llama Stack memory API stores metadata in PostgreSQL, and the LangGraph checkpointer stores graph checkpoints in the same or a separate PostgreSQL instance.
